messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Unemployed
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 42

He is 21, European, recently married, and unemployed, though he does not describe himself that way at first. He says instead that he is “between things,” as if the right next step might still appear if he waits long enough. Most days he is at home with his wife in their small apartment, drifting between late mornings in bed and long evenings in front of the television he rarely follows. The event he returns to, again and again, is not something done to him directly. It is what happened to his wife six months ago, and the fact that he was there to see part of it and helpless to stop it.

They had been married only a few weeks. He remembers that period with a kind of painful brightness: cheap furniture, supermarket flowers on the table, arguments about nothing, the pleasure of calling someone “my wife.” One evening they are walking back from a friend’s place after dark. He is teasing her about how seriously she gives directions, and she is laughing, half turned toward him, when a car comes too fast around the corner. He still tells the story in fragments, as if his mind can only tolerate it in flashes: headlights; her body knocked sideways; the sound of her head hitting the pavement; one shoe in the road without her in it. He remembers screaming her name and then not recognizing his own voice.

At the hospital he sits under fluorescent lights with blood on his hands that is not his. He watches staff move quickly around her bed while no one explains enough. He calls her parents. He signs forms. He tells himself he needs to stay calm so he can be useful, but inside he is convinced she is going to die and that the last thing he did before it happened was make her laugh. For weeks afterward, while she recovers from fractures and a head injury, he lives on adrenaline. He sleeps in a chair beside her hospital bed and jerks awake every time a monitor changes tone. If she closes her eyes too long, he stands to make sure she is still breathing. Nurses reassure him, but reassurance does not settle in. His body behaves as if disaster is always one second away.

When she finally comes home, other people talk about how lucky they are. He nods because that is what he is supposed to say. He is grateful she survived, but “lucky” feels obscene. He begins avoiding the street where it happened, then the whole neighborhood after dark, then any busy road. If his wife needs to go to a follow-up appointment, he insists on accompanying her and becomes tense and irritable before they even leave the apartment. At crosswalks he grips her elbow too hard. If a car takes a corner quickly, his heart slams and he pulls her back sharply, sometimes before there is real danger. Once she tells him, gently, that he is hurting her arm. He lets go immediately and then spends the rest of the day ashamed.

He does not return to job hunting after the accident. Before, he had been sending applications and talking vaguely about warehouse work or delivery driving. Now the idea of being out in traffic all day makes his stomach twist. He tells family he is staying home because his wife still needs help, which is partly true. But even when she is napping peacefully in the next room, he cannot concentrate enough to fill out forms or answer emails. He opens a job listing and suddenly sees the arc of her body in the headlights. At night he dreams in replay: the impact, the shoe, the unnatural angle of her neck. Sometimes the dream changes and she dies before the ambulance comes. He wakes soaked in sweat and reaches across the bed to feel for her shoulder, needing contact before he can believe where he is.

During the day he is on edge in ways he does not fully understand. A siren outside makes him flinch. Brakes squealing in the street below can ruin the next several hours. He scans intersections automatically, even from bus windows or café tables. His wife notices that he always chooses the seat facing the door, with a view of the road. He startles easily and then gets angry at himself for it. The anger spills out elsewhere. He snaps when dishes are left in the sink, when plans change, when relatives say she is “back to normal.” Almost immediately he regrets it and goes quiet. He says less now with friends because ordinary conversations feel unreal and exhausting. When they ask how he is, he says, “Fine, just tired.”

The hardest part for him is the guilt, which has grown larger as the physical emergency has passed. He replays small choices with a punishing precision: if they had left ten minutes earlier, if he had walked on the outside of the pavement, if he had seen the car first, if he had told her not to turn while talking. He knows, logically, that he did not cause the accident. He says this in the flat tone of someone reciting a fact that does not reach his bones. What he feels is that he failed at the most basic task of loving someone—keeping her safe.

In the present, his world has narrowed to routines that help him feel a little less vulnerable. He checks the lock twice before bed. He texts his wife if she is out of his sight for too long. He listens for her footsteps in the apartment and becomes uneasy when it is too quiet. He still loves her with tenderness and fierce devotion, but his love is threaded now with fear. He says he misses the version of himself who could walk beside her without imagining impact. Even on calm days, part of him is braced, waiting for the next terrible thing to happen.
